en: He caressed you like white stallions.
“My fathers Koshoy and Bakai still live,
And many souls have been stirred.
I retied my girdle,
Thinking: ‘If we seize this accursed wretch,
We shall nip him at the source.
If this boy lives,
He will bring strife upon his own nest.’
He was plainly my enemy.
My uncles, Koshoy and Khan Bakai,
Had worn out horses and seen many lands.
A woman’s thoughts grew troubled:
To my eyes, the child I had nursed
Appeared an enemy.
When he sucked my breast,
My heart withdrew and divided;
This deceitful, false world of filth
Seemed no bigger than a fistful.
He was himself a young stalk of the enemy,
The black eye of a foe
Who would ruin the people and ravage the land.
His nature was strange, his venom strong;
He would lay many of us low.
If his daily fortunes prospered,
If this child gained strength and grew,
He would encamp all along Ala-Too,
He would destroy the last of my line,
He would spread slaughter to my borders,
And settle every score with me.
He would leave the country in ruin,
Bring death upon us now,
Do all the evil he was born to do,
And kill every soul without sparing a hair.
His wrath would rise over our heads,
And bring us all to utter ruin.
Gorging and gnawing on rich rump meat,
Fattening as he destroyed my domain,
Trampling and ravaging my borders,
He would revel in this slaughter,
Dragging away the mighty
And wounding them upon the road.
However much I spoke, none understood.
Longing for every sort of evil,
I, the black-faced woman who foresaw it,
Exhausted all my wisdom;
My mind wearied and my heart burned,
And when I stood there helpless,
Straining my wits and pondering,
The light of God in heaven grew overcast,
And sixty cares and a thousand torments
Befell my unfortunate head.
My ribs ached as if torn apart,
And tears poured from my eyes.
‘How could Kanchoro, who sucked my left breast,
Ever become an enemy?’ I wondered.
‘He will devour all who remain,
Turn the river from its course,
Slaughter every living soul,
And do whatever he pleases.’
A fierce flame burst from my body.
From the right breast that Külchoro sucked
Pure white milk gushed forth.
‘He shall ascend the sovereign throne,
And not only he, but his children,
And all his descendants after them,
Shall possess an inheritance that never passes away.’
I knew what he would become;
I knew that the dark-eared, hungry lion
Would become a mighty hero,
And that his fathers and forefathers,
Dark and formidable beyond other men,
Would become an irresistible torrent.
Whenever I thought of Kanchoro,
My heart was pierced and divided.
‘Perhaps he will become a destined enemy’—
I saw this deed before my eyes.
He gathered the Argyn and made them his people,
Reached the wise man and held a feast:
The aged father of the nation,
The saint revered by the people,
The wise and valiant Khan Bakai.
Let kinship be sacrificed,
I have no one to look to but those two.
One day it shows its face,
Another day it shows its flesh—
Such is this filthy world.
I thought she was my good mother,
But she was a shaman mother.
Her speech is plain when she speaks,
Her eyes see beyond this world;
She was my shaman mother.
You were good, dear mother...
But you began your wickedness,
Abandoning to ruin your people,
The many Kyrgyz of Ala-Too.
Knowing and seeing through divination,
You reached your desire long ago.
To the city of Khan Karakan,
You fled, wandering in disgrace;
For this you went roaming away.
You settled on a sheer cliff.
Branded a sorceress,
You earned an evil name.
My gray-wolf mother Kanykey,
Your great knowledge brought you good.
Our honor has departed—
No such tale has ever been heard.
“The child sucked my breast,” you say,
“He sucked it far too hard,” you say,
And make an omen of it,
You wretched, shameless mother,
Creating such a commotion.
Oh child, who can know whether
The baby in the cradle will become a lord?
Who can know whether
The child in the womb will become a khan?
Would the son of this khanly prince
Ever fear a clash of arms?
Child, would the son of a noble prince
Ever be afraid of a child?
Shame, mother, shame—let all hear!
This troublesome, ill-fated boy,
While still too young to grow,
Let us put him to death.
Let us crush his belly beneath our feet,
And renounce all kinship
With this wretched boy.
Let us pour sand into his mouth;
If our hands cannot kill the child,
Let us destroy him utterly,
Make all his days dark,
And find some way to do it.
Then the affairs of the age will prosper,
And such crookedness will vanish.”
Saying these words then,
I sharpened my black tongue
And spoke out before the khan.
“She is only a woman,” they said,
“From time immemorial,
A woman’s deeds have been flawed,” they said,
And hobbled my thoughts short.
“They have become enemies,” they said.
Why should my wretched, dishonored mother
Regard as an enemy
A child still in the womb?
I have no steed but my gray horse,
And apart from Külchoro and Kanchoro,
I have no other kin.
When I stoop, I have no saddle,
And to accompany and support me,
I have no nephew born of an elder sister.
I have no elder brother to uphold me,
No maternal uncle to lean upon,
No younger brother to be my companion.
While Külchoro and Kanchoro,
Those two with rhyming names, remain,
I have no brothers but those two,
And without them I have no life.
What lives today is gone tomorrow;
My heart is aflame, my breast is embers,
All for the two boys with matching names.
“Just see how he lies,” she said,
And because of Kanchoro
She utterly shamed her.
Before all the people, his mother,
The foal of a surging river,
Was left whining like a howling dog.
Venom scattered across my face,
My mouth was sealed and could not open,
My honor scattered like ashes.
My heart burned and became embers,
My mouth faltered before speaking,
Then opened without the slightest movement,
And the fierce words leaving my mouth
Scattered like fire across the earth.
Koshoy and Bakai were there,
Men who had worn out horses and seen many lands,
With heroes of countless kinds,
And all the Kyrgyz people.
My soft-fledged pale falcon,
My morning star born of my own flesh.
You mangled my words,
And brought shame upon me;
You scattered my speech abroad,
And made me a public disgrace.
My wounded pride struck the earth;
The mouth that spoke was stopped.
I, the wretched, dishonored woman,
Breathed only through my back;
Through toil I won my people.
Thirty daughters-in-law and thirty maidens
I sent out to serve me.
I prepared a white, gleaming sword.
I raised an Argyn and made him a man.
While Kanchoro was still a child,
I thought of slaughtering him.
When the trembling sun was setting,
When the people’s herds had settled,
And the folk lay down in peace,
My thoughts departed, wretched as I was.
I opened the hearth and faced the heights—
Who is there to hear these words of yours?
Let the dark and gloomy night hear;
Who else but it can hear?
Your words are not fitting;
Mother, your words came like an enemy’s.
Clear your clouded brow,
And, suffering mother who raised me,
Close your mouth and nose.
Oh, this will bring you shame;
Remain where you are,
For what you contemplate is monstrous.
This deed will bring disgrace;
Stay among those distant people.
My chosen Külchoro,
The banner borne by my spear,
Companion of my khanly father,
The gift of Khan Almambet,
The remnant of my beloved,
The lock upon all I built,
The heart of the marketplace.
These boys are Bagdagül’s morning stars,
The support of my fleshly heart,
The mates of those I have left,
The finest of the beloved ones.
My father’s lion,
The Kyrgyz people’s eagle,
The Chubak of Khan Baltai.
On the rugged forked mountain pass,
With my father, the lion Manas,
He swore friendship for the next world;
He is the beloved of this entrusted soul.
The flower-filled hope of my heart,
The son of my foster-father Chubak—
This Kanchoro is that son.
See how this ill-fated mother of mine
Understands none of this!
She says the infant in the womb
Sucked her breast till she wailed,
And so became her mortal enemy—
My mother, darkened by misfortune.
When he was still an infant,
She had the spirits carefully guard him,
And had costly crimson cloth
Laid over him in splendor.
She appointed sixty blood-shedding champions
To shed blood in his defense,
To rout whoever attacked,
And destroy whoever caused loss.
She set young women to guard him,
And slaughtered barren mares and young camels
To provide for his nourishment.
She had Margalan and Kokon searched,
And red raisins and sweet foods
Brought from every city.
